en: The Book of the Hermitage Dwelling.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory."
While King Yudhiṣṭhira ruled the earth under a single umbrella,
no sound of distress was heard, nor was any beggar ever seen.
When the three worlds were pervaded by the fame of that hero of Dharma,
people became indifferent toward compositions concerning the lineage of Rāghava and others.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with Vidura and the devoted Gāndhārī, constantly regarded them as his deities, even in the absence of their images.
He personally inspected the cooks of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the king who prepared various kinds of side dishes with the six flavors for his meals.
O Kurus, at the command of the elder, all the Pāṇḍavas refrained from doing anything unpleasant;
yet they all offered a retort to him as he spoke such offensive words.
"Let it be proclaimed that the son of Ambikā eats only food fit for a king"—
having thus made this public, he himself secretly subsisted on fruit alone.
Alas! Yudhiṣṭhira did not perceive the world-weariness of that vow-observing reciter, who lay upon the ground with his wife as his companion. (Bhājana 15.8)
As they lived in this manner, full of mutual affection,
fifteen years passed away as time flowed on.
Then, at one point, remembering the wicked conduct of the Kauravas, the furious Bhīma spoke many words concerning their slaughter.
Having heard this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who had conquered his anger, accompanied by his daughter-in-law,
performed everything as if he had never heard it before, and became eager for renunciation.
Then, due to his extreme world-weariness, the mind of that seeker of peace turned away from the delusions of worldly existence and became adorned with dispassion.
For those consumed by hundreds of separations and swallowing the poison of humiliation,
the renunciation of everything is for the sake of happiness alone— a cascading stream of the nectar of nirvāṇa.
Approaching Yudhiṣṭhira, eager for his forest exile, he—
emaciated by his observances and a churner of self-restraint and tranquility— spoke.
"O King, O Pārtha, you who are the preceptor of the castes and stages of life, grant me leave;
I am now going to the forest of asceticism to attain the state befitting an elder."
This delight in the savor of worldly pleasure, for those whose minds are intent upon it,
increases constantly, like an undigested thirst in men.
Touch me with your body of meritorious fragrance, O delighter of Dharma!
May it be well with you; protect the earth and look upon all creatures as your own children.

O protector of the people, you should exert the greatest effort in securing your treasury, fortresses, and army; for when secret counsel is maintained, the royal fortunes of a king remain firmly rooted.
Having spoken thus and smelled the king’s head, the old man— emaciated from fasting and with a trembling body— became eager to depart.
With tearful eyes and palms joined in reverence, the king entreated him:
"How indeed can you leave me behind and go to the forest?"
"I do not venture here to abandon my satisfaction in serving your feet;
for you, O Father, who are free from passion, even this home is a forest of asceticism."
When he did not wake up even though being thus entreated by him,
then the sage, the son of Satyavatī, approached in person.
Approaching the King of Dharma, he whose eye was wisdom spoke:
"O Protector of the Earth, let this old man be released; let him go to the forest of asceticism."
For those whose minds are fully ripened, the supreme fruit at the proper time of learning, age, wisdom, discernment, and noble lineage is dispassion.
When the hair has been whitened by old age and interest in sense-objects has subsided, I consider nothing superior to the forest of asceticism as an ornament for embodied beings.
When Vyāsa had vanished after saying this,
the bull among the Kurus rejoiced at the words "So be it," which the dejected king uttered as if with great difficulty.
Having performed the supreme *śrāddha* for his elders, headed by Bhīṣma,
that noble man gave abundant gifts highly esteemed by the Brahmins.
The sons of Pāṇḍu did not create any obstacle for him as he was giving [the gifts].
But Bhaṅgāsvari, his eyes copper-red with anger, addressed Dhanañjaya.
How can I endure the expenditure of wealth for the *śrāddha* of those Kauravas, by whom terrible sins and many deceptions were committed against us in the past? (Bhājana 15.29)
"Let the wicked Duryodhana go to hell along with his younger brothers;
we ourselves shall perform the funeral rites for the son of Śantanu."
Having repeatedly restrained the son of the Wind who was speaking thus,
Śvetavāhana said, "This must not be spoken again."
Then the king, the son of Ambikā, set forth together with Gāndhārī,
accompanied by Gāvalgaṇi as his companion, having taken leave of the citizens and followed by Vidura.
Though earnestly entreated by her sons and daughters-in-law with tearful eyes,
Kuntī, following the command of her husband, did not abandon her desire for the ascetic grove.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, accompanied by Kuntī and his younger brothers,
entered with a pure heart the forest frequented by royal sages.
There, having met with Śatayūpa, the most excellent of royal sages,
he and his younger brother, wearing matted hair and bark garments, performed austerities for a very long time.
The great seers, Nārada and others, came to see him— who was emaciated by intense ascetic observances— having arrived because they had accomplished their purpose.
Accompanied by all the women of the Bharata lineage, those great chariot-warriors deposited their vast fourfold army at the edge of the forest.
Having set aside their white umbrellas and yak-tail whisks,
they entered the ascetic grove frequented by Dhṛtarāṣṭra on foot.
Having bowed down to the son of Ambikā, as well as to their mother and Sañjaya, they,
being despondent upon seeing those who were reduced to mere sinews, fell into a swoon.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra also inquired about the welfare of the treasury, the citizens, and likewise the countryside, as reported by Sañjaya.
Then, having inquired about the increase in the ascetic merit of the elder of the Kurus, Yudhiṣṭhira asked, "Where is Vidura? And being thus questioned, he replied to him.
Subsisting on air, his limbs reduced to mere bones, wandering at will and naked,
Vidura is seen in this forest, my son, and yet he is not seen.
When Dhṛtarāṣṭra had spoken thus, Vidura approached by chance,
his limbs smeared with dust, his face as large as a wood-apple fruit, and emaciated.
Seeing the people in the hermitage, he became intent on flight;
Yudhiṣṭhira, with tearful eyes, pursued him alone.
Vidura saw him sometimes visible and sometimes invisible;
out of disregard, he regarded those free from passion as equal toward a blade of grass and a king.
Resorting to the foot of a tree, his body blazing as if with wisdom,
he was addressed by the king, who desired conversation, saying, "I am Yudhiṣṭhira."
With unblinking eyes and observing silence, his mental afflictions extinguished upon beholding him,
he quickly and suddenly entered into that very [Buddha] with his eyes, hands, and senses.
When Vidura had entered [the fire], having cast off his body like a snake shedding its skin,
the king abandoned his passionate nature and became filled with knowledge.
Then, as the body of the steward (Kṣattṛ) was prepared to be cremated there,
the sky-dwellers perfected in knowledge restrained Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, having gathered all of that together and reported it to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the monarch remained free from sorrow in the presence of his mother along with his younger brothers.
Subsisting on fruit and sleeping on the ground, he then spent the night;
at dawn, having given as much gold and jewels as they desired to the twice-born, he departed.
Having bowed down to the bull among the Kurus as he sat together with the royal sages,
he beheld the son of Satyavatī, a mass of splendor, who had arrived there.
Vyāsa also, honoring the son of Dharma who stood with palms joined in reverence,
praised that praiseworthy attainment of the Kṣattṛ through the dharma of an ascetic.
He was entreated by Kṣatravṛddha, Gāndhārī,
and Pṛthā for the sake of all those kings who had gone to the other world along with the Kauravas.
Vyāsa showed them the waters of the celestial river to the Kuru women;
even those virtuous wives followed him in celestial chariots, having cast off their physical bodies.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, having stayed there for a month in that place frequented by the Seven Sages, set out for his city at the urging of the elder of the Kurus.
Accompanied by hosts of chariots, horses, and elephants, he proceeded, sighing repeatedly;
as if against his will, he entered the capital with great difficulty.
Then, while the King of Dharma was ruling the earth according to righteousness,
as time passed, the celestial sage Nārada arrived.
Questioned and honored by the king, he spoke of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s story:
"O King, that royal sage has attained the supreme goal."
For one year he subsisted on air, and for another year he abstained from food;
with his face shaped like a ball, he became emaciated and difficult to recognize.
Then that sage, desiring liberation and free from ritual action, abandoned the fires;
they, too, continued to exist in the forest thick with ancient trees.
There, the high-minded king, accompanied by his beloved consort Kuntī,
seeing the forest ablaze, entered into supreme meditative absorption.
Unobstructed, all-pervading, pure, and with their own mental activities dissolved,
they entered the supreme abode through the openings of the manifest universe.
Thus, for them, the tree of knowledge has borne fruit: its sprout is tranquility, its shoots are the renunciation of everything, and its flower is the light within one's own mind.
Then, consumed by that forest fire as if by a kinsman,
Sañjaya, emaciated by his vows, departed for the mountain of snow.
Having heard this, the son of Pāṇḍu, pervaded by the fire of grief,
lamented along with his younger brothers for Kuntī and the bull of the Kurus together with his sons.
Then, after the celestial sage had departed, the king performed the water-libation rites and,
dedicating them to those very [ancestors], bestowed vast and inexhaustible wealth.
Then, having taken hold of fortitude and cast off the grief born of the body,
he meditated upon the worthlessness of cyclic existence and took refuge in discernment.
All phenomena are by their very nature fragile; the mind attached to them cannot endure the remorse that comes with separation.
Therefore, for embodied beings struck by the poison of parting from what is dear, vast discernment is in every way the nectar that brings peace.
Thus ends the Āśramavāsika Parvan in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Śrī Kṣemendra.
